alternative: an explicit while/for loop with reassigned locals, LINQ Aggregate for a collection fold, or an explicit Stack<T>/Queue<T> worklist when the recursion is not tail-recursive
implementation_notes: C# has no tail-call guarantee: the IL tail. prefix exists (System.Reflection.Emit.OpCodes.Tailcall) but the C# compiler never emits it, and even hand-emitted IL has it ignored in some cases, so ordinary methods always take a frame per call. Deep recursion therefore ends in StackOverflowException, which .NET documents as the exception thrown when the execution stack exceeds its size - and which cannot be caught, so the failure is a process abort. The realization of the pattern is its loop form: the accumulator becomes a local, the recursive call becomes an assignment plus continue, the base case returns.
idiom_name: explicit while loop with reassigned locals (Roslyn emits no tail. prefix)
pitfalls: StackOverflowException is not catchable in .NET: a de facto tail-recursive method that is not rewritten aborts the process instead of failing one operation.
Iterative rewrites that keep an explicit Stack<T> move the memory from the managed stack to the GC heap - a crash becomes allocation pressure, which still needs a bound.
Recursion through async/await is never a tail call: the awaited continuation is stored on the heap and the depth moves into memory, so async walks must be loops as well.
